title: Exponential Growth and Decay: Functions, Compound Interest and Models

meta_desc: Free Algebra 1 exponential growth and decay worksheets (F-LE.A.1, F-LE.A.2, F-IF.C.8b): read y = a(b)^x, evaluate exponential functions, linear vs exponential tables, write models, compound interest and depreciation. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: y = a(b)^x: start at a and multiply by b each step.
key_sub: Growth: b = 1 + r. Decay: b = 1 − r. Linear adds; exponential multiplies.
body_html:
How it works

An exponential function has the form y = a(b)x. a is the initial value (when x = 0) and b is the number you multiply by each step. If b > 1 it is growth; if 0 < b < 1 it is decay.

For a percent change, b = 1 + r (growth) or b = 1 − r (decay): 6% growth → 1.06; 15% decay → 0.85. Compound interest: A = P(1 + r)t.

Linear functions add the same amount each step; exponential functions multiply by the same amount.

Example

Write a model: 600 rabbits, growing 8% a year.

a = 600, b = 1.08.

Answer: y = 600(1.08)t

Example

A $20,000 car loses 15% a year. Value after 3 years?

b = 0.85.

20,000 × 0.853 = 20,000 × 0.614125.

Answer: $12,282.50

Example

Find f(3) for f(x) = 4(3)x.

33 = 27 first.

4 × 27.

Answer: 108

Common mistakes

  • Using 0.15 for a 15% decrease. The value left is 85%, so use 0.85.
  • Reading b = 1.04 as a 104% rate. The rate is 0.04 = 4%.
  • Adding the rate each year (linear) instead of multiplying.
  • Multiplying a × b first: 4(3)3 is 4 × 27, not 123.

faq.q: How do you tell exponential growth from decay?
faq.a: Look at the base b in y = a(b)^x. If b is greater than 1 it is growth; if b is between 0 and 1 it is decay.

faq.q: How do you find the growth rate from y = 500(1.04)^t?
faq.a: Subtract 1 from the base: 1.04 − 1 = 0.04, so the growth rate is 4% per period.

faq.q: What is the compound interest formula?
faq.a: A = P(1 + r)^t, where P is the starting amount, r is the yearly rate as a decimal and t is the number of years.

faq.q: How can I tell if a table is linear or exponential?
faq.a: If the outputs go up by the same amount each step it is linear; if they are multiplied by the same number each step it is exponential.
